reply_text:
Checking how the War Machine's cascades already use patterns, to compare with the causal-model version.㊥ (does it fit?) Probably yes, and more directly than I expected. The War Machine already reads each pattern as a small open model. Each pattern gets a guard, made of tokens it `:needs` and tokens it `:forbids`, plus the tokens it `:produces` (`cascade_decision.clj:84`). The ordering between patterns is built the same way the branch's `glue` joins models: pattern A sits above pattern B when A produces a token that B's guard needs (`construction.clj`, as checked in PROOF-2a-PLAN). So a cascade is already small pieces joined on shared token names. What the causal reading would add is the set of questions you can ask of the joined whole. There are three places where the two don't match yet.

🈖 (the correspondence) A WM pattern reading converts almost mechanically into an `open_theory/theory`:
- its produced tokens are the variables it owns;
- the mechanism for each is "all `:needs` and none of the `:forbids`";
- the needed and forbidden tokens are its inputs, listed as its outputs to other patterns.

Joining the patterns gives one causal model for the whole cascade. You could then ask of it:
- which patterns the want actually depends on, which is the set of causes the branch computes for R;
- the counterfactual "would the cascade have reached its want without pattern X?";
- the joint independencies, which are predictions to check against what clicks actually did.

The WM doesn't compute any of these today. Its feedback counts per pattern whether the pattern was selected or verified as enacted. This also bears on the branch's own stated limit, that its models are authored by hand. In the WM, the readings come from R6's interpretations at run time, so the joined model would be built from data rather than written.

㊟ (where it doesn't fit yet)
1. **Two producers of one token.** In a cascade, several patterns can produce the same token, and the WM simply takes the union. `glue` refuses that as `:double-mechanism`. A cascade version would make each token the OR of its producers' firings. That is a small, deliberate change, but it is a change.
2. **Time and repetition.** A cascade is a rollout over steps, and tokens accumulate. A causal DAG has no cycles and is fixed. Patterns that feed each other would have to be unrolled per step, or `glue` refuses with `:cycle`.
3. **Probability.** The WM scores cascades with rates, posteriors and G. The branch's models are true/false only. Probabilistic mechanisms are the next tier up in M-diagramprover (D3), registered but not built. For structure and counterfactuals, true/false is enough. For anything that feeds G, it isn't.

🈖 (the giant connected cascade) PROOF-2a-PLAN records your why/how split: outcome wants are `:role :why` and lifecycle exits are `:role :how`. It also records that these terms are kept so they can link to the cascade you're building in M-象-2000, with no link built yet. Patterns as causal models would supply that link: the why/how tokens become the shared names the pieces join on. A large model made of small ones is exactly what `glue` produces, and it refuses with a reason when the pieces don't fit.

㊭ (a cheap way to find out) Take the interpretations from one recorded click's cascade, convert each pattern into an open model with the OR rule from point 1, and join them. Then report three things:
- whether they join, and if not, which refusal and on which token;
- the causes of the want;
- one counterfactual that removes a pattern.

This is read-only and needs no WM change. It would tell us whether the fit holds on real cascades or only on the hand-written Kimi case. It needs the branch on master first, or it can be run on the branch in its own process.

🈸 (one decision) Shall I try that on one click?

previous_reply_acts.text:
(what the skeleton computes)
- **Derivation of R.** The report → constrain → propose chain comes out as the set of causes of the commit. The mission had reconstructed this by hand from session order.
- **The `:反事实世界模型` hole.** If the guard pattern had been in force, there would have been no red tape. The joined pattern models serve as the world model that ARGUE-0 said was missing.
- **Withdrawal semantics.** The two possible wirings give different answers. Under the gate as built, which never reads rule records, withdrawing the rule record leaves the red tape in place. If enforcement read the record, withdrawing it would stop the red tape.
- **The capture drop.** It comes out causally independent of the requisition commit. That holds only for these five patterns; adding a pattern that links them would change it.
- **103 implied independencies.** These are predictions the act history could falsify. None has been tested yet.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (limits it states itself) The models are written from the mission's text, not mined from the store. Values are true/false only, with no probabilities. Variables are matched by name. I haven't run its tests. The commit reports 71 tests passing and four planted bugs caught.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(relation to M-aif-over-the-operator and today's MAP)
- **Withdrawal.** The withdrawal result is the same distinction our mission draws between a `:withdrawn` record and what the machine actually does. A record can change what gets reported without changing what gets enforced.
- **Two other routes to patterns.** Its item "Patterns that predict" turns each flexiarg into a causal model whose independencies can be tested against the act history. Our pattern-bidding route found that patterns barely line up with operator turns, which is part of why we went to keywords. This is a different route: it tests patterns against what happened, not against what you said.
- **S8 and offers.** S8 would join an arriving act into the model before it lands. That fits the offer pipeline: an offer with an action class is exactly such an arriving act.
